# BigQuery Query Optimization: Myths vs. What Actually Saves Money

I’ve spent over a decade working with BigQuery, watching it mature through many feature releases. It abstracts away an enormous amount of complexity, but not all of it. If you have spent any time in the real world with it, you have met the standard BigQuery query optimization checklists. Name your columns instead of using SELECT *. Filter on the partition column. Avoid CTEs. Cast your join keys.

You nod, refactor your SQL, and check the results. Sometimes nothing happens. Sometimes the execution time drops but the billed cost stays exactly the same. In the worst cases you waste hours on a recommendation that does not apply to your environment.

Generic advice treats all optimizations as equal. They aren’t. Here is what “BigQuery Query Optimization” means in this article:

- BigQuery (the environment). Your pricing model dictates your reality. On-demand bills bytes scanned; Capacity bills compute slots over time. Cutting bytes might not help your slot consumption, and an optimization built to reduce slot-ms can just as easily increase your byte footprint.

- Optimization (cost vs. time). Cost or latency? Sometimes an engineering decision, sometimes a business one. A query that runs in 5 seconds instead of 50 is a technical victory, but if it scans the same 30 TB on On-demand, you have saved nothing on your BigQuery bill.

- Query (the scope). We think of queries as SQL: the SELECT, JOIN and WHERE clauses. But an AI agent, a BI tool or a dbt macro is generating most of it, and you cannot rewrite what you do not author. Query optimization often means changing a layer below the query text.

Implementing query optimizations in BigQuery that actually save you money and improve performance requires understanding five layers and the most effective query optimization techniques: partition pruning, column pruning, sampling and sketches, result caching, history-based optimizations, materialized views, data models and storage optimization. In this article, I include examples of optimized SQL queries, best practices, and uncover BigQuery query optimization myths with real numbers.

## The Five Layers of BigQuery Query Optimization

Whether a SQL tweak becomes a win depends on the layers stacked below it and the pricing model you are in. For more on pricing: “ Making Sense of BigQuery Pricing Models: On-demand, Capacity, Editions ”.

I call them the five layers of BigQuery query optimization:

- Predicates: where you filter. A filter on a partition column before the scan decides how much data BigQuery ever touches; the same filter after a join only decides how much comes back. It lives inside one query, so it is the cheapest thing on this list to change.

- Scope: how much of the table you ask for. Columns and rows, independent of any filter: SELECT * bills every column whether you read it or not, and an exact distinct count bills the whole table when an approximation would do.

- Engine: what BigQuery already does for you. The result cache, history-based optimizations, and everything the service does unasked. You do not write this layer, you qualify for it, so the work is removing what disqualifies a query: a nondeterministic function, or a shape that changes just enough each run to learn nothing from the last. Free when it fires, and rarely checked.

- Precompute: reusable models you build and maintain. Materialized views, aggregate tables, and the models sitting between raw tables and the queries that read them. It pays once and then charges rent: it saves on every read and has to be refreshed and kept correct, so it needs a well thought out design to earn its place.

- Storage: partitioning, clustering, and column layout. How the bytes sit before any query arrives. Pruning cannot prune a table that was never partitioned, so the slowest layer to change is also the one that caps what the other four can do.

Each layer gets before-and-after examples and a way to measure it yourself. The techniques mapped to each are non-exhaustive; more can be added as you refine your architecture and as BigQuery ships new features.

In this article we will walk these layers from the outside in: from the layers where most people spend their time until we reach the storage one that decides whether any of the outer ones are possible. Keep this value ordering in mind as you read this article, because it runs almost exactly opposite to the effort ordering.

First, the techniques divide by the resource they save: bytes for On-demand, slot-hours for capacity. Some sit on the boundary, because fewer bytes scanned means less data for an aggregate to work with.

Second, ownership dictates execution. The outer Predicates layer is a free-for-all populated by analysts, dbt models, BI tools and now AI agents. The foundational layers (Engine, Precompute and Storage) are usually governed by the data engineering team.

That gives us a law for BigQuery query optimization, based on our model: inner layers set the ceiling, outer layers spend it. Let’s look at what this can mean in practice. For instance, trying to prune data in a WHERE clause saves nothing on an unpartitioned table. Column pruning is hard-capped by the physical byte layout of the columns themselves. An extreme example of this is that if you have only one deeply nested JSON column, you will not get any benefits of columnar layout and pruning. The deeper you go, the harder the change is to deploy: a predicate change at the edge is a pull request, modifying a clustering key at the core is a table migration.

Let’s start at the very edge, and work inwards.

### PREDICATES: Where you Filter

The outermost edge. Cheapest layer to change, most familiar to analysts, and the only layer most generated SQL ever touches. Because everyone has access to the WHERE clause, it is also where myths are created.

#### Partition Pruning

A partitioned table only saves you money if BigQuery can work out which partitions it needs at planning time. Everything that defeats pruning does so for one reason: if the planner is forced to execute logic per row to find the partition, it scans the entire table.

The Anti-Pattern: Defeating the Planner

-- Blocks pruning: the function must be evaluated per row

SELECT * FROM `bigquery-public-data.crypto_ethereum.transactions`

WHERE FORMAT_DATE('%Y-%m-%d', block_timestamp) = '2020-01-01'

Because a function is wrapped around the partition column, the planner is blind. It cannot know the result without reading the row first, so this triggers a full scan: BigQuery reads all 132 months to find the single day you asked for.

The Fix: Clean Pruning

-- Prunes cleanly: identical rows returned, planner sees the literal bounds

WHERE block_timestamp >= '2020-01-01'

AND block_timestamp < '2020-01-02'

Both return the same rows. Because the second compares the partition column directly against literals, the planner discards every other partition before reading a byte.

Isolating the partition column on one side of your operator is the gold standard, but BigQuery does not always force raw literals. The planner accepts a whitelist of built-in functions and formats ( docs ): with constant secondary arguments it prunes through DATE_TRUNC, TIMESTAMP_ADD and EXTRACT, and it parses FORMAT_TIMESTAMP with exact specifiers like %Y-%m-%d. Step outside that whitelist and the optimization breaks silently. The docs support %Y-%m-%d for FORMAT_TIMESTAMP, which leads many to assume FORMAT_DATE behaves the same way. It doesn’t.

Never assume the engine will figure it out for you. BigQuery is full of small gotchas, trust me. Use a dry run to verify your WHERE clause is actually pruning bytes.

Pre-join Filters

Filtering before a join is usually sold as “fewer rows are cheaper”. True, and it misses the point: the real goal is dropping one side under the broadcast threshold. Feed 138 million rows into a join, as in the animation, and BigQuery defaults to a shuffle join , redistributing both sides across every slot so matching keys land together, moving enormous amounts of data across the network. Pre-filter one side far enough and it flips to a broadcast join , replicating the small side to every worker instead, and network movement drops to near zero.

BigQuery's own optimizer is awake, though. The myth says to always pre-filter in subqueries, which implies it does nothing. BigQuery uses predicate pushdown, moving filters as close to storage as possible before data is retrieved, so on a standard INNER JOIN rewriting a plain WHERE into subqueries frequently changes nothing.

Manual pre-filtering earns its keep only where the planner cannot push down by itself:

- A null-extended side of an OUTER JOIN.

- Complex query interactions where predicates span multiple operations or both sides of the join.

- Predicates filtering over aggregate, limit, or window results.

Miss one and all 138 million rows go straight into that shuffle.

### SCOPE: How Much of the Table you Ask for

Which columns you pull and how many rows you request. Both are declared explicitly by you, billed before the engine runs the query, and visible in a dry run, which makes Scope the cheapest layer to verify.

#### Column Pruning

The animation above profiles bigquery-public-data.stackoverflow.posts_questions. A query for two columns against a lazy SELECT * is nearly 50 times fewer billed bytes for the same answer.

What the visual makes obvious is how unequal the columns are. Dry-run all twenty individually and one text column, body, turns out to be 90.1% of the table’s physical footprint.

SELECT * is rarely expensive because it reads twenty columns. It is expensive because it drags that one massive column along for the ride. Before you burn hours rewriting forty queries to trim a few lightweight INT64 fields, find your table’s body column first.

The complex type trap. BigQuery’s columnar storage prunes native STRUCT fields, so querying nested_col.single_field only pays for that leaf. You pay for the whole structure if you SELECT nested_col at the root, or if the data is JSON, where extracting one key forces a full scan of the string.

LIMIT is an illusion. LIMIT 10 restricts what is returned to your screen, not what is read from disk. Adding it on the end of a SELECT * does nothing to reduce bytes scanned.

#### Sampling and Sketches

If LIMIT does not make querying cheaper, BigQuery offers two options that do, balancing precision against performance and cost. They are distinct techniques used for different reasons.

TABLESAMPLE: bounding the bytes. As the animation shows, a sample rate reduces the bytes read from disk in proportion to the rate you ask for. At the low end it does better than proportional: ask for 1% and you might be billed for 0.66%, because SYSTEM sampling reads whole randomized blocks rather than individual rows.

Why use it : Discovery, and the development loop. Nobody re-runs a finished, perfect query twenty times, but everybody re-runs the one they are still writing. Or the one to check the schema, even though they shouldn’t.

Sketches: bounding the error and the compute. Where sampling restricts how much data is read, a sketch restricts the CPU and memory needed to aggregate it. BigQuery uses HyperLogLog++ for distinct counts and KLL for quantiles, available on wrappers like APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT. Sketches can also be extracted, stored in a table and merged later, turning a repeated full-table aggregation into a cheap re-aggregation.

Why use it : production reporting where exactness is not necessary but speed is. Note: a sketch saves compute, which a dry run cannot show you.
